questions.question: The settings screen has three buttons that show only a picture. We are rewriting the labels so that someone using a screen reader hears what each button does. The three pictures, from left to right, are a bin, a padlock and a printer. Which set of names should we use?

options.label: Name the action
options.description: Call them Delete file, Lock account and Print. The meaning is clear without seeing the picture, but the names are longer than the words on the picture.

options.label: Name the picture
options.description: Call them Bin, Padlock and Printer. Quick to write and to test, but a reader who does not know the pictures learns nothing.

options.label: Say nothing at all
options.description: Leave the buttons unnamed and rely on the position on the screen. The list stays short, but a screen reader announces only Button, with no purpose.

options.label: Say position only
options.description: Announce First, Second and Third instead of a purpose. Stable between releases, but the reader must guess what each button changes.

questions.question: The app labels mix two languages: Arabic (تُرجَم الواجهة من اليمين إلى اليسار) and Hebrew (הממשק נקרא מימין לשמאל), with English product names such as Studio kept as they are. We need one written rule so translators and developers agree. Which rule goes in the guide?

options.label: Follow the sentence
options.description: The line follows the language of the sentence, and English names sit inside it. Best for reading comfort, but every screen needs extra testing.

options.label: Always left to right
options.description: Lay every label out left to right, even in Arabic. Simple to build and to test, but Arabic sentences then read in the wrong order.

options.label: Guess from characters
options.description: Let the layout work out the direction from the characters it finds. Almost no work to set up, but the guess fails when a line mixes Arabic and numbers.

options.label: Mirror the whole screen
options.description: Flip the layout, arrows and icon positions together. Matches what Arabic readers expect, but charts and code samples can end up backwards.

questions.question: Which changes should the next version of the agreement include? Choose every one that applies. Our service agreement is 4,200 words long. It covers what the account is for, what we promise, what we do not promise, how the account is closed, what happens to stored items after the account closes, how complaints are handled, and how the rules may change. A reading check with 20 volunteers found that 14 stopped before the complaints section and 9 could not say what the phrase reasonable notice meant in practice. Short sentences and named sections help most of these readers, but each change has a cost. Which change should be made first?

options.label: Rewrite and split
options.description: Cut every sentence to under 20 words and split the text into named sections with a contents list. Helps nearly every reader, but needs a legal review and about three weeks.

options.label: Add a summary page
options.description: Add a one page plain summary above the full text and leave the rest as it is. Fast to publish and easy to measure, but readers who want detail still meet the same wall of text.
options.preview:
**Plain summary**
- one page at the top
- full text unchanged below
- test with 5 readers

options.label: Add a glossary
options.description: Explain words such as reasonable notice in a list at the end. Cheap and useful for new readers, but it does not shorten a single paragraph.

options.label: Offer a phone read
options.description: Let someone ask a staff member to read the agreement aloud on the phone. Best for readers who find long text hard, but it uses staff time and helps only callers.

questions.question: A help article about a forgotten password currently says: Utilise the aforementioned credential reset utility to re-establish your authentication token prior to accessing the portal. In a test, most readers stopped at the word aforementioned and none of them could say what to click. Which replacement should the writer use?

options.label: Use everyday words
options.description: Write Reset your password to get back into your account. Easy to read and to translate, but the new words must also be used in the buttons on the page.

options.label: Keep it, add a link
options.description: Leave the sentence as it is and add a link to a simpler page. Nothing needs rewriting this week, but the hard sentence stays where every reader meets it.

options.label: Add a small glossary
options.description: Explain credential, authentication token and portal in a box under the paragraph. Cheap and quick, but readers still have to get through the jargon first.

options.label: Use a picture instead
options.description: Replace the sentence with a labelled screenshot of the reset screen. Helps many readers, but the screenshot needs a long description before it helps screen reader users.

Two are blocking: the date picker cannot be reached with a keyboard, and the booking confirmation is shown only as a green flash with no text. The work runs as three stages: stage one sets the list of problems, stage two fixes them, and stage three checks the fixes. The same four approaches are offered at every stage. Choose the approach to use for each stage.

options.label: Alternative 1
options.description: Alternative path for stage 1.

options.label: Alternative 2
options.description: Alternative path for stage 1.

The work runs as three stages: stage one sets the list of problems, stage two fixes them, and stage three checks the fixes. The same four approaches are offered at every stage. The work runs as three stages: stage one sets the list of problems, stage two fixes them, and stage three checks the fixes. The same four approaches are offered at every stage. Choose the approach to use for each stage.

questions.question: The results screen shows three states as coloured dots with no words: 🟢 delivered, 🟠 returned, and 🔴 lost in transit. About one in twelve men cannot tell the amber dot from the red one. How should the states be shown?

options.label: Colour and a word
options.description: Keep the dot and add the word under it, for example Delivered. Works for every reader and for screen readers, but the row is slightly taller.

options.label: Shape and a word
options.description: Use a different shape for each state and keep the colour. Distinguishable without colour at all, but new shapes take a designer and a legend to explain.

options.label: New colour set
options.description: Pick a new palette that passes the contrast check for colour blindness. No change to the layout, but it does not help anyone using a screen reader.

options.label: Remove the dots
options.description: Show only the word for each state and drop the colour. Simplest and clearest, but staff who scan quickly lose the fast visual cue.

options.label: Add a key below
options.description: Keep the three dots and add a small key under the list explaining each one. Cheapest change, but a reader has to find the key before the list makes sense.

questions.question: A twelve minute staff training video has spoken English, a quiet hum of machines, and a person spelling their own name. We must add captions this month. Which caption set should we publish?

options.label: Full human captions
options.description: A trained writer captions the words, names and important sounds, and checks the result against the audio. The best accuracy, but it costs the most and takes about a week.

options.label: Auto then check
options.description: Automatic captions first, then a person fixes names, jargon and the quiet background sound. Good accuracy for less money, but the checking pass still needs an hour of staff time.

options.label: Automatic only
options.description: Publish whatever the tool produces within a day. Very fast and nearly free, but names come out wrong and the quiet sound is never mentioned.

options.label: Summary captions
options.description: Write five short lines that summarise the video instead of transcribing it. Very quick and easy to follow, but deaf viewers lose the exact wording and any detail they need to quote.

questions.question: When a reader zooms the page to 400 percent, the ticket list scrolls sideways and the right hand column goes off the screen. A person who uses a screen magnifier cannot read the dates. What should the team change first?

options.label: Stack the columns
options.description: Turn the two columns into one long list when the page is narrow. Everything stays on screen at any zoom, but the page becomes longer to scroll.

options.label: Reduce the font
options.description: Set the default text two sizes smaller so more fits at high zoom. A quick change with no layout work, but it pushes the text below the size many older readers need.

options.label: Warn about zooming
options.description: Show a message asking people not to zoom. Almost no work, but it tells a reader with low vision that the tool is not built for them.

options.label: Offer a plain page
options.description: Build a second, simpler page for large text only. Helps people who find the first page hard, but the two pages can drift apart over time.

questions.question: The benefits page ends with: Failure to comply with the verification requirements may result in the immediate suspension of your claim without prejudice to any other remedies available under these conditions. The page is also published in an easy read edition. Which closing line belongs in the easy read edition?

options.label: One short sentence
options.description: If we cannot check your details, we may stop your claim. Easy to read and to translate, but it leaves out the other remedies that the full version mentions.

options.label: Keep it, add a note
options.description: Leave the full sentence and add one plain line under it. Nothing legal changes, but the reader still meets the long sentence first.

options.label: Split into bullets
options.description: Break the sentence into four short bullet points, one clause each. Clearer than the original, but easy read guidance usually asks for even shorter wording.

options.label: Point to an adviser
options.description: Replace the paragraph with an invitation to call an adviser. Easiest to follow, but it does not tell the reader what will actually happen to their claim.

questions.question: In the photo gallery, the next and previous arrows only respond to a mouse click, and tabbing skips the whole gallery. A keyboard user cannot see any photo beyond the first. Which fix should be written into the ticket?

options.label: Use real buttons
options.description: Turn the arrows into ordinary buttons so tabbing reaches them and Enter or Space works. Fixes the problem for everyone, but the styles need a small redesign.

options.label: Add swipe support
options.description: Let the arrows respond to a swipe on a tablet. Helpful on touch screens, but it does nothing for a desktop keyboard or a switch device.

options.label: Add a text link
options.description: Put a plain link called View all photos in a list above the gallery. Keyboard users can reach the list, but the gallery itself still stops working.

options.label: Auto advance the slides
options.description: Move through the photos on a timer so nothing needs clicking. Removes the keyboard barrier, but it cannot be paused and it moves too fast to read.

options.label: Add a text photo list
options.description: List every photo title as text under the gallery. Gives a screen reader and a keyboard user a real way through, but it has to be kept in step with the gallery.

options.label: Explain the gallery keys
options.description: Add a line telling keyboard users which keys move between the photos. Cheap, but it only helps people who already know the gallery exists.

questions.question: Choose every change that should be made to the date field. You may pick more than one. A Braille display shows the page heading as ⠓⠑⠇⠇⠕ but shows the date field as ⠼⠲⠲⠼⠼ with no punctuation between the parts. A user reports that the heading is fine and the date is confusing. What should the team do about the date field?

options.label: Speak the separator
options.description: Have the field announce a pause between the parts, for example year, pause, month, pause, day. Clear on a Braille display, but it changes the punctuation other screen readers already read.
options.preview:
**Braille note**
- announce year, pause, month, pause, day

options.label: Use the full date
options.description: Show 2026-03-14 in the ISO order everywhere in the field. Short and unambiguous in Braille, but many readers find the numbers harder to read aloud.

options.label: Add a text label
options.description: Show the date in numbers and add the words Date of birth in the label. Works for every output, but it does not change the punctuation problem in other fields.

options.label: Fix the Braille only
options.description: Change only the text sent to the Braille display. No risk to sighted users, but two versions of the same field will drift apart over time.

questions.question: A public meeting is streamed online. Sign language interpretation is already in the room, but the online stream carries only the room sound. Roughly a fifth of the online audience relies on the stream. Which addition should be funded?

options.label: Interpreter picture in picture
options.description: Put the interpreter video in the corner with a clear name attached. Follows the room, but the interpreter's hands can be small and the main speaker's voice can be louder.

options.label: Signed recording
options.description: Record a separate signed version of the meeting and publish it beside the audio. Clearer to watch at any size, but it can take two weeks to produce and goes out later than the meeting.

options.label: Automatic captions
options.description: Add automatic captions to the audio stream. Almost free and quick, but automatic captions are weak on names and council jargon.

options.label: Transcript afterwards
options.description: Publish a written transcript the next day. Useful for searching and quoting, but it arrives after people have already made up their minds about the meeting.

questions.question: A product photo carries the description: image of a product. The photo shows a blue kettle with a handle on the left and a white lid. Which description should replace it?

options.label: Describe what it shows
options.description: A blue kettle with a white lid and a handle on the left side. Useful for a screen reader user choosing a kettle, but it does not say the material or the price.

options.label: Use the file name
options.description: img_0041_kettle_blue_final.jpg. Short to write automatically, but it tells a screen reader user nothing about the picture.

options.label: Describe the whole scene
options.description: A staged kitchen photo with a blue kettle, a mug and a window behind. Rich context for an article, but far too long for a shop product list.

options.label: Mark it decorative
options.description: Tell the screen reader to skip the picture. Removes noise for people who browse in list mode, but a shopper who cannot see loses all product information.

revision.feedback: Keep the six word rule for shop photos, then send me a second pass that adds material and size as separate short sentences.

questions.question: When a form is sent with one missing box, the page says: Error 4027: invalid data supplied by user. The reader has no idea which box is wrong, and the error appears at the top of a long page. Which message should replace it?

options.label: Name the field and fix
options.description: We could not read your date of birth. Enter it as 14 March 2026. Names the box and shows the expected format, but the page still has to scroll the reader back to it.
options.preview:
**Error copy**
> We could not read your date of birth.
> Enter it as 14 March 2026.

options.label: Add a top list
options.description: Keep the short error and add a summary box at the top that links to every problem. Helps keyboard and screen reader users, but the summary must be kept in step with the fields.

questions.question: The sign-up form asks for Name, Address and Postcode, and the first box has the placeholder Full legal name. Placeholders disappear as soon as anyone starts typing, so a screen reader user hears nothing when they return to the box. Which wording change fixes it?

options.label: Permanent label above
options.description: Put Your full name above the box and keep it there while typing. Always available to every reader, but the form grows taller and needs a layout change.

options.label: Longer placeholder text
options.description: Make the placeholder longer and clearer, for example Enter your first name and last name. No layout change, but the text still vanishes on the first keystroke.

options.label: Hidden label attribute
options.description: Add a label that only the screen reader can see. Fixes the announcement with no visual change, but sighted keyboard users gain nothing and the hidden text can drift.

options.label: Example under the box
options.description: Keep the placeholder and add an example line under the box, such as Jane Okonkwo. Concrete help for everyone, but the field still has no permanent name.

options.label: Label plus example
options.description: Put a permanent label above the box and keep an example under it. Best of both, but the form needs extra vertical space on every screen size.

questions.question: Two counters at the service desk have a hearing loop, but visitors cannot tell which ones work. Signs exist at the desk but are behind the glass. What is the smallest change that helps?

options.label: Signs on the counter
options.description: A small loop sign on the surface of each counter that has a working loop. A visitor knows before they sit down, but the signs need replacing whenever a loop is repaired.

options.label: Ask at the counter
options.description: Front desk staff ask every visitor whether they want the loop. No new signs, but it depends on the member of staff saying it every single time.

options.label: Mark the floor
options.description: Paint a clear route and label the loop counters on the floor. Visible from a distance, but it is easily blocked by a queue and needs re-painting often.

options.label: Note it on the website
options.description: Mention the loops on the venue page of the website. Free to update, but a visitor standing at the desk has no way to read it.

questions.question: The signup has nine steps. In a trial, 41 of 60 readers dropped out between step five and step six, which asks for three bank details at once. The steps are labelled 1 of 9 through 9 of 9 with a forward arrow → on each. Which change best reduces the drop out?

options.label: Split the bank step
options.description: Ask for one bank detail per screen and keep the step count the same. The hardest screen becomes easy, but the form feels even longer than nine steps.

options.label: Remove some steps
options.description: Cut the nine steps to five by removing fields nobody uses. Shortest and simplest, but research is needed to be sure the removed fields are not required later.

options.label: Add a progress bar
options.description: Show a bar and write how long it will take, for example about four minutes. Readers often keep going, but it does not fix the hard bank screen itself.

options.label: Allow saving midway
options.description: Let a reader stop at step five and get a link to finish later. Helps people with limited time or energy, but people with no email cannot use it.

questions.question: A skip link is placed before the main menu, but it stays invisible on screen, so a sighted keyboard user presses Tab, sees nothing change and presses Tab again. How should the link behave?

options.label: Show it when focused
options.description: The link becomes visible as soon as it takes focus, then moves the reader to the main content. Standard practice and easy to test, but it needs a clear colour that meets contrast rules.

options.label: Remove the skip link
options.description: Delete it because the menu is short. Simplest code, but keyboard users must tab through every menu item on every page.

options.label: Leave it hidden
options.description: Keep it invisible and rely on screen reader support. Works for screen reader users, but sighted keyboard users get no clue that focus has moved.

options.label: Add a keyboard shortcut
options.description: Add a shortcut key that jumps to the main content. Powerful for expert users, but the shortcut itself has to be learned and documented.

questions.question: The welcome screen slides in from the right, with the arrow ➜ wiping across the text. Several readers have reported dizziness when the animation runs. What should the default be?

options.label: Follow the setting
options.description: Read the reader's reduced motion setting and replace the slide with a simple fade or nothing at all. Respects the choice with no new setting to design, but a fade may still need checking.

options.label: Make the slide shorter
options.description: Cut the animation from four seconds to under one. Less dizziness, but the setting is ignored for readers who have asked for no motion at all.

options.label: Add a stop button
options.description: Put a small stop button in the corner of the animation. Gives control back, but a reader who cannot see the button never finds it.

options.label: Keep the animation
options.description: Keep the slide because the brand team prefers it and add nothing else. No work, but it works against a setting the reader has already chosen.

revision.feedback: The reduced motion setting has to be read by the page, with a manual stop as a backup, before this ships.

questions.question: The word Owner appears in the property tool, the finance tool and the help centre, and next to it the same label is written in Arabic, للمالك, and in French, propriétaire. Translators have used three different words across the three languages we support, and readers keep asking whether they mean the same person. What should the team publish?

options.label: One agreed glossary
options.description: Fix one approved translation for Owner and about 40 other shared words, and require all three tools to use it. Readers learn one word, but the list needs a named owner and a review each year.

options.label: Translate in each tool
options.description: Let each tool choose the word that reads best in its own context. Reads more naturally, but the three tools then disagree and support gets more tickets.

options.label: Add a tooltip
options.description: Explain the word where it appears, in the language of that screen. No glossary to maintain, but a tooltip is easy to miss and is not read by every screen reader.

options.label: Keep English only
options.description: Leave the words in English and translate only the sentences around them. Cheapest to maintain, but readers who cannot read English are left guessing at the key noun.

questions.question: Which of these search behaviours should we offer? Choose every one that we should build. A reader typed Müller into the search box and got no result, although the record is stored as Müller. The same happens in reverse for Björk and Nguyen. Which behaviour should the search offer?

options.label: Ignore accents when searching
options.description: Treat Müller and Muller as the same search, in both directions. Forgiving and easy to explain, but it can match two different people with similar names.

options.label: Exact first, then loose
options.description: Try the exact spelling first, then quietly retry without accents if nothing is found. Precise and forgiving, but the retry takes a moment and must be explained in the help text.
options.preview:
**Search order**
1. exact spelling
2. same word without accents

options.label: Offer a switch
options.description: Add a checkbox called Ignore accents. Readers choose, but one more control to explain, and it is off by default for most people.

options.label: Require the accents
options.description: Ask the reader to type the accents exactly. Simplest for the database, but it blocks people using a keyboard or a phone that cannot type the marks.

questions.question: The editor has nine shortcuts, listed only in a help panel that appears when the mouse rests on the title bar. A keyboard user who opens the panel by keyboard cannot see it. How should the help be shown?

options.label: Always visible list
options.description: Show the list in the help panel whenever it is opened, by mouse or by key, and announce how many items it holds. Reaches every reader, but it takes space on a small screen.

options.label: Printable cheat sheet
options.description: Publish a one page cheat sheet that can be printed and stuck by the keyboard. Useful for people who like paper, but it is not available inside the tool itself.

options.label: Show once on first use
options.description: Show the list the first time someone presses a shortcut. Low intrusion, but it appears at the worst moment and most people dismiss it without reading.

options.label: Hover tooltips
options.description: Keep tooltips on the buttons and add them to the shortcut list. No layout change, but hover alone excludes keyboard and touch users.

questions.question: On the results page, the archive button and the delete button are both announced as Remove. A screen reader user hears the same word twice in a row and cannot tell which is which. What is the correct fix?

options.label: Make the names specific
options.description: Announce Archive item and Delete item, so the object and the action are both clear. Standard practice and easy to test, but the buttons get wider on screen.

options.label: Add the row context
options.description: Keep the short names but have the screen reader add the item name from the row, for example Remove, invoice 402. No visual change, but it depends on the table structure being read correctly.

options.label: Keep only one
options.description: Remove the archive button and keep only delete. Simplest for the reader, but it removes a function people rely on and loses the ability to undo.

options.label: Leave them the same
options.description: Keep both names as Remove and rely on the row position. No work, but the ambiguity stays for every screen reader user.

questions.question: This notice runs to 340 words in a single block: You must notify us in writing within twenty eight days of the date of the decision letter if you believe that the decision was made in error or that the information we used was incomplete or out of date, and if you do not do so the decision stands and any later request will be treated as a new claim which may be affected by the time limits that apply to new claims rather than to reviews of this decision. Readers say the paragraph is hard to follow. What should the editor do?

options.label: Split and number the steps
options.description: Break it into three numbered sentences under plain headings, and keep the legal wording intact. Big readability gain for a small amount of editing work, but the exact phrasing is preserved only in the small print.

options.label: Cut to the deadline
options.description: Keep only the twenty eight day rule and delete the rest. Very easy to read, but the reader no longer learns what happens if they miss the deadline.

options.label: Add an audio version
options.description: Record the paragraph and let readers listen. Useful for people who struggle with dense text, but it does not help a screen reader user who is scanning for the deadline.

options.label: Bold the key words
options.description: Make the twenty eight days and the two grounds bold. Very fast, but bold alone does not make the sentence order any easier to follow.

questions.question: Which changes should be made to the help page? Choose every one that applies. On the help page the headings run: Help centre, then Services, then Book a place, with no level in between. Some screen reader users use the heading list to skip around, and the jump means the middle item disappears from that list. What is the smallest correct change?

options.label: Insert the missing level
options.description: Add one heading at the level between, for example Browse services, so the steps go one at a time. The smallest change that fixes the structure, but it needs a new heading and a matching menu entry.

options.label: Change the size only
options.description: Make Book a place look smaller in the design without changing its level. No new words, but the structure a screen reader relies on is unchanged.

options.label: Bold the second heading
options.description: Make Services bold so it reads as a parent. Common in print, but bold text is not a heading as far as a screen reader is concerned.

options.label: Add a menu instead
options.description: Add a contents menu at the top of the page with links to all three. Helps people who scan, but the heading structure that breaks the skip list is still wrong.

questions.question: An order screen shows only a row of emoji: 📦 🕒 ✅. A screen reader announces package, clock, check mark, with no words at all, so nobody knows what the three symbols mean. What should replace the row?

options.label: Keep emoji, add words
options.description: Show the emoji and the word beside it, for example Packed, In transit, Delivered. Clear for everyone and still friendly, but the row needs more space on a small screen.

options.label: Words only
options.description: Replace the symbols with three short words and no pictures at all. Fastest for a screen reader, but staff who scan quickly lose the visual cue they are used to.

options.label: Hidden names for emoji
options.description: Keep the emoji and attach a spoken name to each one. No visual change, but sighted screen reader users get help while sighted users still get symbols only.

options.label: Keep the emoji
options.description: Leave the row unchanged and explain it in the help page. No work on the screen, but the ambiguity stays on the screen people actually read.

questions.question: This paragraph appears in a benefits letter: You are required to return the enclosed form within twenty eight days of the date of this letter together with evidence of your circumstances, failing which your award will be suspended and any payment already made may be recovered. The letter is also produced in an easy read version. Which rewrite belongs in the easy read version?

options.label: Three short lines
options.description: Send us the form. Send it within 28 days. Add proof of your situation. If we do not get it, your payments may stop. Easy to read, but the recovery of past payments is only hinted at.

options.label: Keep it, add words
options.description: Keep the legal paragraph and add the short version underneath it. Both readers are served, but an easy read page is meant to replace dense text, not to add to it.

options.label: Two columns of text
options.description: Set the same paragraph in two narrow columns to make the lines shorter. Purely visual, but the sentence is still one long chain of clauses.

options.label: Phone number instead
options.description: Replace the paragraph with a phone number and opening hours. Very easy to act on, but a reader who is not near a phone learns nothing about the deadline.

questions.question: A results table has ten columns and no header row. A screen reader user hears ten numbers in a row with no idea which is the date and which is the amount. What is the best fix?

options.label: Mark the header row
options.description: Turn the top row into real column headers so each cell is announced with its column name. The standard fix, but the ten columns are still very wide on a phone.

options.label: Split into two tables
options.description: Show one table for dates and one for amounts, each with its own header row. Much easier to follow, but readers have to hold two lists in their head.

options.label: Offer a list view
options.description: Add a button that shows the same data as a list of sentences, one row per line. Very readable, but it is a second view to build and to keep in step.
options.preview:
**List view**
1. Invoice 402, 12 March, 45 pounds
2. Invoice 403, 14 March, 90 pounds

options.label: Add more spacing
options.description: Put blank space between the columns to make them easier to follow visually. Helps sighted readers, but the spoken output is unchanged.

options.label: Add a download option
options.description: Offer the same data as a spreadsheet download for readers who prefer a file. Useful for analysis, but a spreadsheet is not read aloud in any helpful way.

options.label: Remove two columns
options.description: Cut two rarely used columns so the table is eight wide instead of ten. A real improvement, but it removes information that a few readers rely on.

questions.question: In a captioned safety video, the narrator says only watch the screen, while an important alarm noise and a flashing red light carry the warning. Captions record speech only. What should the team add?

options.label: Describe the sounds
options.description: Add bracketed lines such as alarm sounds and red light flashes. Deaf viewers then get the whole warning, but the caption writer must watch the screen as well as the script.

options.label: Transcribe the script only
options.description: Keep captions as speech only, which is the normal rule. Cheapest, but the two non spoken warnings are lost for every Deaf viewer.

options.label: Add audio description
options.description: Add a spoken description of the flashing light for sighted viewers. Helps low vision readers, but it does nothing for Deaf viewers.

options.label: Add a warning page
options.description: Put a written warning above the video. Cheap and clear, but it cannot be timed to the moment the alarm sounds.

questions.question: The cookie banner has a small cross in the top corner. Its hidden name is Close. A screen reader user hears Close cookie banner, Close dialog, Close button in turn and cannot tell what each one does. What should the hidden names say?

options.label: Say what each closes
options.description: Use Accept cookies, Refuse cookies and Close this message. Each name says what it does, but the names are longer and must be translated into every language.

options.label: Keep the short names
options.description: Keep Close and rely on the surrounding words to give the context. Short and quick to translate, but a reader moving quickly still hears the same word three times.

options.label: Use the icon alone
options.description: Use only the cross with no name at all. Fewer announcements, but an unnamed control is effectively invisible to a screen reader user.

options.label: Point to the heading
options.description: Make each control read the banner heading before its own name. More context, but long announcements slow down every pass through the banner.

questions.question: On the checkout page, tabbing goes logo, first field, the payment logo, then back to the second field, because the payment logo sits early in the code but late on the screen. Which change fixes it?

options.label: Match code to screen
options.description: Put the controls in the code in the same order they appear on the screen. The correct fix, but it means rewriting part of the page structure.

options.label: Set the tab numbers
options.description: Add explicit tab numbers so the payment logo comes last. A quick fix, but large tab numbers cause real problems the next time a control is added.

options.label: Remove the payment logo
options.description: Take the payment logo out of the focus order because it is only a picture. Simple, but the picture then becomes a new set of small tab stops to check.

options.label: Leave it as it is
options.description: Leave the order alone and add a note in the help text. No rework, but every keyboard user meets the same wrong order on every checkout.

questions.question: The save button is a light grey on a white page. A contrast tool gives it 2.1 to 1, and the accessibility rules ask for 4.5 to 1 for body text. Which change should the designer make?

options.label: Darken the button
options.description: Use a dark grey that reaches 4.5 to 1 and keep the white text. One colour change and the button passes, but the change must be checked on every page that uses it.

options.label: Make the text larger
options.description: Enlarge the label until it counts as large text, which allows 3 to 1. Cheap, but a large label on a small button looks wrong and the fill still fails on its own.

questions.question: A claim is refused with this text: your application does not satisfy the qualifying criteria as defined in schedule two. The reader is not sure what schedule two is or what the criteria are. What should the new wording say?

options.label: Name the criterion
options.description: You do not meet rule 4 in schedule two, which asks for a receipt dated in the last three months. Clear and specific, but the rule has to be rewritten for every kind of claim.

options.label: Point to a help page
options.description: Add a line pointing to a help page that explains schedule two. One line of work, but a reader who has just been refused should not have to go and find it.

options.label: Keep the legal wording
options.description: Keep the exact legal wording and add a summary beneath it. Safe for the legal team, but the reader still meets the hard sentence first.

options.label: Offer a phone call
options.description: Offer a callback where an adviser explains the refusal. Very helpful for many readers, but it needs a phone number the reader can use.

questions.question: The home page carousel moves by itself every four seconds and there is no pause control. A reader with a vestibular condition reports nausea. What is the correct change?

options.label: Stop the automatic move
options.description: Remove the timer so the slides only change when the reader asks. The most reliable fix, but the design team loses an effect they consider lively.

options.label: Add a pause control
options.description: Add a pause button and show it on every slide. Gives control back, but a reader must find the button before the first move, which is already uncomfortable for some people.

questions.question: A site notice reads: All activities are undertaken at your own risk and the organisation accepts no liability for any loss howsoever caused. Readers ask what that means for them in practice. Which rewrite is clearest?

options.label: Say it plainly
options.description: You are responsible for your own safety on the site. We are not responsible for injuries or lost property. Plain and honest, but the legal team will want to check the exact wording.

options.label: Keep it, add a note
options.description: Keep the legal sentence and add a short note under it. Both versions exist, but readers see the hard sentence first every time.

options.label: Highlight key words
options.description: Keep the sentence and make own risk and no liability bold. Quick, but bold does not tell a reader what either phrase means.

options.label: Remove the notice
options.description: Take the notice down because the insurance covers most cases anyway. No hard text, but the organisation may be legally required to display it.

questions.question: Saving a form works silently: the button greys out and nothing is said. A screen reader user presses save and hears nothing, so they press it again and again. What should be added?

options.label: Speak the status
options.description: Add a short spoken status, for example Saved at 14:05, in a place the screen reader will notice. Clear for everyone, but it must not interrupt a reader mid sentence.

options.label: Show a written banner
options.description: Show a written message at the top of the form that stays until the next change. Visible to all readers, but a screen reader user may not hear it unless it is also announced.

options.label: Change the button text
options.description: Change the button from Save to Saved once the save works. Free and obvious, but it only works if the reader looks back at the button.

options.label: Leave it silent
options.description: Leave the save silent because most people watch the button. No work, but the repeated pressing problem stays for screen reader users.

questions.question: A page uses a small blank picture as a gap between two sections. It has the description small blank image, so a screen reader stops and reads it. What is the correct description for that picture?

options.label: Mark it as empty
options.description: Give it an empty description so the screen reader skips it completely. Standard practice, but the gap then disappears for screen reader users, who navigate by structure instead.

options.label: Describe the gap
options.description: Give it a description such as space before the next section. It makes sense on its own, but announcing a gap every time adds noise to every pass through the page.

options.label: Remove the picture
options.description: Delete the picture and create the gap with page styling instead. The cleanest outcome, but every place that uses the picture must be found first.

options.label: Keep the description
options.description: Keep small blank image as the description. No work, but every screen reader user hears it for no reason.

questions.question: A line in the Arabic interface, تاريخ الجلسة (14/03/2026), shows a date and a bracket in the wrong order, so the closing bracket appears before the text. The stored text is correct; only the display order is wrong. What should be fixed?

options.label: Isolate the mixed text
options.description: Wrap the number and the bracket so the layout treats them as one block. A small, correct fix, but every place that mixes languages must be found.

options.label: Fix it by hand
options.description: Add invisible spacing characters around the number by hand. Works in the one place it is applied, but it breaks the moment a translator edits the line.

options.label: Left align the whole line
options.description: Force the line to be left aligned so the order looks right. It hides the problem, but the reading order is still wrong for a screen reader.

options.label: Remove the brackets
options.description: Take the brackets out of the design and use a divider line instead. Nothing to order wrongly, but brackets carry meaning in two other places on the page.

questions.question: The booking page says your request is in the queue and will be processed in due course. Readers do not know whether to wait or phone. Which wording should replace it?

options.label: Give time and step
options.description: We will reply within 5 working days. If you have not heard from us by then, call the office. Clear and actionable, but the office has to be ready for extra calls.

options.label: Say only pending
options.description: Your request is pending. Shorter, but still leaves the reader without a date or a plan.

options.label: Give a rough estimate
options.description: Most requests take about two weeks. Sets an expectation, but a firm promise is deliberately avoided, so readers still cannot plan around it.

options.label: Offer an update email
options.description: Send an email as soon as the request is decided. Good for people who cannot check the page, but it does not answer the question at the moment of reading.

questions.question: A screen reader reader moving through the address form hears the labels but never hears Personal address and Work address, so the two blocks of fields blur together. What should be added?

options.label: Group with a named set
options.description: Wrap each block in a group with a heading that is spoken, such as Personal address. Standard practice and it survives future edits, but the layout needs two small visual changes.

options.label: Just make the text bold
options.description: Keep the headings but make them bold and larger. Looks like a heading, but a screen reader treats it as ordinary text and will not announce the group.

options.label: Repeat group in labels
options.description: Write Personal address, line 1 in each field label. No grouping needed, but the repeated words make every field announcement long and noisy.

options.label: Split the page in two
options.description: Move the work address to a second page. Clearly separated, but it adds a step and readers lose the chance to see both addresses at once.

options.label: Show a visible heading
options.description: Show the group heading on screen as well as to the screen reader. Visible to everyone, but it needs a style change in two places on the form.

questions.question: A status bar shows four emoji with no words: ✅ ⚠️ ❌ ⏳. A screen reader reads check mark, warning, cross, hourglass, and a reader has no idea which state is blocking their order. What should be added?

options.label: Add a word to each
options.description: Put a short word next to every symbol, such as Done, Needs attention, Blocked, Waiting. Clear for all readers, but the bar is wider and the words need translating.

options.label: Replace with words
options.description: Remove the symbols and show only four short words. The simplest output, but the quick visual scan that many staff rely on is lost.

options.label: Add a legend once
options.description: Explain the four symbols in a small key shown when the bar is focused. One key to write, but it has to be found and read before the bar makes sense.

options.label: Keep the symbols only
options.description: Keep the four emoji and add a note in the internal handbook. No change on screen, but the same confusion reaches every customer who looks at it.

questions.question: The introduction to a repair form says: It is important to note that the form should ideally be submitted at the earliest convenience, ideally in duplicate where possible. What should the writer do?

options.label: Delete the padding
options.description: Remove the sentence entirely and keep the instructions that follow. Very clear, but the writer must check nothing useful was hiding inside the padding.

options.label: Shorten it to one line
options.description: Rewrite as Send this form as soon as you can, ideally a second copy. Keeps the meaning, but the word ideally still leaves a reader unsure whether a second copy is required.

options.label: State it as a rule
options.description: Rewrite as Send two copies. Nothing about ideally, so the requirement is unambiguous, but it may be stricter than the office actually needs.

options.label: Keep the sentence
options.description: Keep it because formal tone is expected in official forms. No edit, but the reader still has to decode the wording before acting.

options.label: Use short sentences only
options.description: Keep the requirement but split it into two short sentences with no hedges. Plain and quick, but the word ideally is still needed to say a copy is helpful, not required.

questions.question: A message bar appears at the top of the page after 5 seconds and disappears again after 12, with no close control. A screen reader user is still reading when it vanishes. What should change?

options.label: Do not hide it
options.description: Leave the message on the page until the reader dismisses it. Nothing disappears unexpectedly, but the bar takes space on small screens and needs a close control.

options.label: Give it more time
options.description: Extend the display from 12 seconds to 60. A simple change, but a slow reader is still cut off and the timing is still a guess.

options.label: Pause while focused
options.description: Keep the timer but freeze it while the message has focus or while the reader is inside it. Fair to screen reader users, but the behaviour is hard to explain.

options.label: Keep the timer
options.description: Keep the twelve second timer because the message is not important. No work, but a message that arrives and vanishes unheard helps nobody.

questions.question: Two records for the same person are stored differently: one uses é as a single character and the other uses e followed by an accent mark. Search finds only the first. What should the search do?

options.label: Normalise on save
options.description: Put every new record into one form when it is saved and compare search words in the same form. One record per name, but existing data must be converted once and reviewed.

options.label: Normalise on search
options.description: Leave the stored data alone and normalise only the words being searched for. Smallest change, but a name typed the other way round still finds nothing.

options.label: Leave records unchanged
options.description: Keep both forms because they are technically different strings. No work, but the same person appears twice and support cannot tell which record is current.

options.label: Search both spellings always
options.description: Run four searches for every typed word, one for each accent combination. Finds the most matches, but it is slow and can return unrelated names.

questions.question: A label in the Arabic interface reads اسم الملف معروف also by two names, with the English words placed at the start of the line. The line displays in the wrong order. What is the correct approach?

options.label: Wrap the Latin words
options.description: Mark the Latin words so the layout keeps them in reading order inside the Arabic sentence. The correct fix for a mixed line, but it has to be done wherever languages are mixed.

options.label: Translate the names
options.description: Write the two names in Arabic script so the line is a single direction. Simplest to lay out, but it breaks names that must stay in their original spelling.

options.label: Names on own line
options.description: Move the two names onto a second line below the Arabic sentence. Order is safe, but it changes the design and adds a line to every label.

options.label: Force one direction
options.description: Force the whole label to follow the language of the interface and let the mixed words be. No code changes, but the English names end up in the wrong order.

questions.question: A parking page says: Refunds are issued where a cancellation is notified by the applicant, subject to the availability of staff, within fourteen days of the original booking. Which rewrite is clearest?

options.label: Two short sentences
options.description: Tell us if you want to cancel. We will refund you within 14 days if we have staff to do it. Plain and honest, but the staff condition may make some readers angry and is easy to drop by mistake.

options.label: Bullets for the conditions
options.description: Keep the sentence and list the three conditions as bullets under it. The conditions become scannable, but the main sentence is still a single long chain.

options.label: Remove the staff condition
options.description: Rewrite as We will refund you within 14 days of a cancellation and drop the staff clause. Very clear, but it promises something the office may not always be able to deliver.

options.label: Keep the original
options.description: Keep the original sentence and add an example under it. Familiar to legal writers, but readers still decode the same sentence.

questions.question: The Arabic interface shows prices with Western digits, 120.50, while some older screens use Arabic digits ١٢٠٫٥٠. Readers report confusion between the two. Which format should the new screens use?

options.label: Match the language
options.description: Use Arabic digits in Arabic screens and Western digits in English screens, as each language does in print. Familiar to readers, but the same value looks different in exports and reports.

options.label: Always Western digits
options.description: Use 0 to 9 everywhere, which is also what the payment system expects. Consistent across the product, but some older readers find the forms unfamiliar.

options.label: Let the device decide
options.description: Take the digit shape from the phone or computer settings. Respects each reader's preference, but the same page looks different to the person standing behind them.

options.label: Show both forms
options.description: Print both, for example 120.50 alongside ١٢٠٫٥٠. Removes all doubt, but it doubles the number text on every price line.

questions.question: A help page opens with: This section outlines the procedural framework governing eligibility determination. Readers skip the rest of the page. What should the opening line be?

options.label: Say who can apply
options.description: You can apply for this if you live in the borough and your income is under 32,000 a year. Gives the reader the answer in one line, but the detailed conditions then need a list below.

options.label: Name the topic only
options.description: Eligibility rules for this scheme. Short and accurate, but it still does not tell a reader whether they qualify.

options.label: Keep the formal line
options.description: Keep the formal opening and add a contents list under it. Standard practice, but the first line still tells a reader nothing about their own situation.

options.label: Link to a checker
options.description: Open with a link to an online checker that tells a reader whether they qualify. Very useful for many people, but it does nothing for readers with no internet access.

questions.question: A comment box rejects text that contains curly quotation marks, such as “smart quotes” or an em dash — and the reader is told the text is invalid. What is the correct behaviour?

options.label: Accept the text as typed
options.description: Accept curly quotes, dashes and ellipses as ordinary text and store them unchanged. The reader can type freely, but any system that compares text must now match smart quotes too.

options.label: Convert when pasted
options.description: Change curly quotes to straight ones as the text is pasted, before the reader sees it. Keeps the old data rules, but the text changes under the reader and the pattern can be a surprise.

options.label: Remove quotation marks
options.description: Strip all quotation marks and dashes from the text. Simple and safe, but it silently alters what the reader wrote.

options.label: Keep rejecting the text
options.description: Keep the current rule and improve the error message. No data change, but readers on phones, where the keyboard produces curly quotes automatically, keep losing their text.

questions.question: A name field rejects a full name that looks correct on screen. After inspection the text contains a zero width space between the two words, and the name is written in Arabic, السماء, which makes the hidden character hard to notice. What should the service do?

options.label: Clean it as it arrives
options.description: Remove invisible formatting characters from pasted text before it is accepted, and tell the reader the name was cleaned. Solves the problem for everyone, but a real name that needs such a character is rare and would be altered.

options.label: Warn and let reader fix
options.description: Show a message saying the name contains an invisible character and ask the reader to retype it. Nothing is changed behind their back, but most readers cannot see the character and give up.

options.label: Accept text as typed
options.description: Accept the text including the hidden character. No friction, but search and matching for that name will fail later without explanation.

options.label: Block all pasting
options.description: Stop readers pasting into the field at all. Removes the source of the problem, but pasting a name from an email is a normal and useful thing to do.

questions.question: The search box shows only a magnifying glass and the placeholder Search. A screen reader announces an editable text field with no name. What should be added?

options.label: Visible label above the box
options.description: Put Search this site above the box so the name is always announced. Clear to every reader, but it adds a line above the header area on every page.

options.label: Label only for screen readers
options.description: Add a name that only the screen reader can see, so the field is announced as Search. No visual change, but sighted users get no extra help and the name must be kept in step.

options.label: Keep the placeholder
options.description: Keep Search as a placeholder and rely on the surrounding header text. Free, but the field is still announced without a name once typing starts.

options.label: Name the button instead
options.description: Give the search button the name Search the site and leave the box unnamed. Some improvement, but the box a reader types into is still anonymous.

options.label: Name the two results
options.description: If you do not come and you do not tell us, we will close your registration and you will go to the back of the list next time. Clear about both consequences, but blunt.

options.label: Name one result
options.description: If you miss an appointment without telling us, we will close your registration. Short and clear, but the effect on future bookings is hidden, which feels unfair later.

options.label: Keep the original wording
options.description: Keep the original wording and add a short version in a box. Both versions exist, but the reader meets the formal sentence first.

options.label: Soften the wording
options.description: Soften it to you may lose your place if you do not come. Gentler to read, but may hides a real consequence behind the word may.

questions.question: A policy message says: Staff will greet you 👋🏽 and use 👍🏽 to confirm your booking. Darker skinned readers say the message looks as though it is about them. What should the team do?

options.label: Use the neutral emoji
options.description: Replace them with the plain waving hand 👋 and plain thumb 👍, which most keyboards offer. Fair to everyone, but some devices still show a skin tone by default.

options.label: Drop the emoji
options.description: Remove the emoji and write the sentence in words. Completely neutral, but the message loses the friendly tone the team wanted.

options.label: Let readers pick a tone
options.description: Add a setting that lets each reader choose the skin tone for emoji across the site. Respectful and personal, but it adds a setting most readers will never find.

options.label: Keep the tone
options.description: Keep the current emoji because they render correctly on staff phones. No change, but the complaint from darker skinned readers stands.

questions.question: A notice gives fees in a five column table with the heading Fees payable. A reader on a screen reader cannot follow the columns. What should replace it?

options.label: One sentence per fee
options.description: Write each fee as its own short sentence, for example A replacement card costs 12 pounds. Reads well aloud, but it takes more vertical space and loses the quick comparison.

options.label: Two column table
options.description: Reduce the table to two columns, the item and the price, with a real header row. Keeps the comparison and works with a screen reader, but long item names wrap a lot.

options.label: Keep the table
options.description: Keep the five column table and add a note saying it is also available as a list. No rewrite, but a screen reader reader still has to fight the columns.

options.label: Publish as a picture
options.description: Publish the table as a picture of the table. Looks tidy, but a picture of a table cannot be read aloud at all.

questions.question: A job advert says he or she must be able to lift 20 kilos and will be required to man the front desk. One candidate, who writes 他、她 style pronouns, was asked twice to reword their application. What should the advert say?

options.label: Use they and staff
options.description: Rewrite as they must be able to lift 20 kilos and will be needed on the front desk. Inclusive and short, but the phrase they will be needed reads slightly oddly in some languages.

options.label: Use the word candidate
options.description: The successful candidate must be able to lift 20 kilos and will work on the front desk. Neutral, formal and easy to translate, but it is more abstract for some readers.

options.label: Keep he or she
options.description: Keep he or she because it is the established house style. No search work, but readers who asked to be included still are not.

options.label: List many pronouns
options.description: Write he, she, they and others in the advert. Shows intent clearly, but the list can read as a box ticking exercise rather than a job description.

questions.question: A flood risk map shows zones in pale blue, pink and green with the names in tiny text. A reader with low vision and colour blindness cannot tell the zones apart. What should change?

options.label: Add patterns and a key
options.description: Give each zone a different pattern, a bold name and a thick outline. Works without colour and at high zoom, but the map needs redrawing by a designer.

options.label: Use stronger colours
options.description: Replace the pastels with three colours that pass the contrast check. A quick change, but it does nothing for a reader who cannot separate those colours at all.

options.label: Add a list below
options.description: Add a written list of the zones and their risk level under the map. Useful for everyone, but a reader using a screen reader has to jump between the list and the picture.

options.label: Keep the map
options.description: Keep the map and rely on the postcode search box. Simple for most people, but the map is still the part screen readers and low vision readers rely on.

questions.question: A left hand menu lists Manage, Configure and Settings, which three different teams use to mean different things. Readers cannot tell which part of the site they are in. What should the menu say?

options.label: Name the task
options.description: Use names like Your details, Payment method and Email choices, each of which is one thing a reader recognises. Clear, but it means renaming items that other parts of the code refer to.

options.label: Group with headings
options.description: Keep the three names but put them under clear section headings so the position tells the reader where they are. Less rewriting, but the names stay vague inside each group.

options.label: Rename only Settings
options.description: Rename just Settings to Your account and leave the other two. The most complained about name is fixed, but Manage and Configure stay as vague as before.

options.label: Keep all three names
options.description: Keep the menu as it is because the three words match the names used in the manuals. No change, but the on screen confusion continues.

questions.question: A delivery note says: Should you not receive the parcel within two working days of the recorded delivery attempt you must contact the depot quoting the tracking number in order for a reattempt to be arranged. What should the note say instead?

options.label: Numbered steps
options.description: 1. Wait two working days. 2. If nothing arrives, call the depot. 3. Give them the tracking number. Each step is one job, but the depot number still has to be printed somewhere on the note.

options.label: One short sentence
options.description: Call the depot within two working days if the parcel does not arrive. Short, but it drops the instruction to quote the tracking number, which slows the call down.

options.label: Keep it, bold the days
options.description: Keep the original and make two working days bold. Very fast, but the sentence structure is unchanged and still hard to follow.

options.label: Link to a help page
options.description: Replace the paragraph with a link to a help page about failed deliveries. One line of work, but a reader holding a paper note cannot follow a web link.

questions.question: A language picker shows 🇬🇧 for English, 🇫🇷 for French and 🇩🇪 for German, and no option at all for Arabic or Urdu. Which change should be made?

options.label: Use written language names
options.description: Write the name of each language in that language, with no flags. Neutral and standard practice, but a reader who cannot read the script still needs a transliteration.

options.label: Keep flags, add names
options.description: Keep each flag and add the written name beside it. Familiar to many readers, but a flag can still suggest a country rather than a language.

options.label: Add every missing flag
options.description: Add flags for the missing languages so every option looks the same. Consistent, but flags for languages spoken across many countries are misleading.

options.label: Group by country instead
options.description: Group the options by country and show a flag for each country. Matches how people think about languages, but it multiplies the list length.

questions.question: A video player has three unlabelled buttons: a triangle, two vertical bars and a rectangle. A screen reader announces button, button, button. What should each be named?

options.label: Name them as actions
options.description: Call them Play, Pause and Full screen, so the name says what the button will do. Standard practice and clear, but the names change when the button changes function, so play becomes pause and must be tested.

options.label: Remove the controls
options.description: Take the controls off the page and let the video autoplay. No announcements at all, but nobody can pause or enlarge anything.

questions.question: A small business is told: Your application does not currently meet the risk criteria applicable to this product category. What should the plain version say?

options.label: Name the rule and gap
options.description: For this product we need two years of trading history and your application shows 14 months. Names the rule and the gap, but it may not be true for every application and needs checking.

options.label: Name the category only
options.description: Your application is not in the category we can offer this product to. Shorter and always true, but it leaves the business with no idea what to change.

options.label: Offer an adviser call
options.description: Keep the refusal short and offer a fifteen minute call with an adviser. Practical next step, but it assumes the business can spare fifteen minutes on the phone.

options.label: Keep the formal wording
options.description: Keep the formal wording because it matches the other letters. Consistent, but the business learns nothing about how to apply again.

questions.question: A maths page shows the formula x ≥ 15,000 in a translated version, and the symbol and digits are pushed to the far left away from the words. What should be changed?

options.label: Mark formula as one piece
options.description: Treat the symbol, the sign and the number as a single piece of text so it stays together and in order. Correct in every language, but every formula on the site has to be marked.

options.label: Write it in words
options.description: Write x is greater than or equal to 15,000 in words. Readable by a screen reader in any language, but it looks less like a formula to sighted readers.

options.label: Align the formula left
options.description: Align the formula to the left edge of the page in every language. Simple layout fix, but the reading order is still broken for a screen reader.

options.label: Formula as a picture
options.description: Publish the formula as a picture. Looks tidy and prints well, but a screen reader user cannot read it and it will not be translated.

questions.question: A 400 word notice mentions the deadline in sentence nine, buried in a paragraph about eligibility. Readers report missing it. What should the editor do first?

options.label: Put the deadline first
options.description: Start the notice with Reply by 30 April 2026 in a bold first line, then give the detail below. One sentence moved, and it is the change most likely to be noticed.

options.label: Bold it where it is
options.description: Leave the paragraph structure and make the date bold where it appears. No rewriting, but readers who skim the first line still miss it.

options.label: Add a reminder later
options.description: Keep the notice as it is and send a reminder two weeks before the deadline. Catches people who read it, but it assumes an email address on file.

options.label: Shorten the whole notice
options.description: Cut the notice to 120 words and include the date in the shortened version. Best overall readability, but it takes longer than moving one line.

questions.question: A Turkish reader searches for Izmir while the record is stored as İzmir with a dotted capital. Search returns nothing, even though the reader spelled it correctly in Turkish. What should the search do for Turkish?

options.label: Match the Turkish rules
options.description: Match the two forms of the letter when the interface language is Turkish, while other languages keep the general rule. Correct for Turkish readers, but it needs a language aware search.

options.label: Match one direction only
options.description: Always convert the letter to one form on both sides of the search. Simple and safe, but it makes search in Turkish less accurate for dotted and dotless pairs.

options.label: Match exactly
options.description: Require the exact spelling with no conversion at all. No code change, but a Turkish reader searching in their own script finds nothing for many names.

options.label: Ignore all dot marks
options.description: Remove all dot marks from both the stored name and the search word before comparing. Finds the widest set of matches, but it can match names that are genuinely different.

questions.question: A price table writes Standard — 45 pounds per year and the dash is read out in some screen readers as a pause, a dash and a second pause. What should the table use instead?

options.label: Use a column
options.description: Put the price in its own column with the package name in the first column, so no dash is needed at all. The clearest result and better for a screen reader, but the table needs rebuilding.

options.label: Use a short dash
options.description: Replace the long dash with a short dash, for example Standard - 45 pounds. A one character change, but some screen readers still read the dash aloud.

options.label: Hide the dash
options.description: Keep the dash on screen but stop it being read out. No visual change, but sighted screen reader users and sighted non screen reader users then see different information.

options.label: Keep the long dash
options.description: Keep the long dash and add a note under the table. No rework, but the awkward reading remains every time the table is read aloud.

questions.question: A form says: Enter your national insurance number in the format AA 00 00 00 A, for example QQ 12 34 56 C. Which version is easier to act on?

options.label: One real example
options.description: Show one clearly valid example, such as QQ 12 34 56 C, and say the letters are two letters then a number. Readers copy the shape, but a two letter first pair may not exist in the real scheme.

options.label: Keep the format code
options.description: Keep the format code and both examples exactly as they are. Consistent with the printed form, but a reader who is not sure which part is the letters guesses and gets rejected.

options.label: Spell the letters out
options.description: Write two letters, then two numbers, then two numbers, then two numbers, then a letter, in words as well as the code. Very clear, but the line becomes long and the two forms can disagree.

options.label: Remove the help text
options.description: Remove the format note and let the service show the error if the number is wrong. The shortest form, but a rejected submission wastes a paper application for many readers.

options.label: Show help under the box
options.description: Put the format and one example under the number box, where the reader is looking. Well placed, but it has to be shown and hidden without hiding the label.

questions.question: A name field accepts 20 characters, but readers with long family names, such as الشيخ عبد الرحمن, are cut off mid word. What is the best change?

options.label: Raise the limit to 100
options.description: Allow up to 100 characters and show a count as the reader types. Almost nobody is stopped, but a long limit makes it harder to spot a mistake before saving.

options.label: Split into two boxes
options.description: Use two boxes, First names and Family name, each with 50 characters. Matches most paperwork, but readers with a single long name have nowhere to put the rest.

options.label: Let it cut and warn
options.description: Keep the 20 character limit but warn the reader when the name does not fit. Fast, but the reader is blocked and has to call for help.

options.label: Keep the current limit
options.description: Keep the limit because the downstream system cannot take more. No change, but the same readers are excluded every time they use the form.

questions.question: A letter opens with: Further to our correspondence of 3 March, please find enclosed the aforementioned documentation. What is the plain replacement?

options.label: Say what is enclosed
options.description: We spoke on 3 March. The forms you need are in this letter. Short and clear, but it drops the word documentation that staff search for in the archive.

options.label: Name the specific forms
options.description: We spoke on 3 March. Please complete the two blue forms inside. Tells the reader exactly what to do next, but it assumes the letter always contains two forms.

options.label: Keep the formal opening
options.description: Keep the formal opening because it matches other letters from the team. Consistent, but readers decode the same sentence on every letter.

options.label: Add a subject line
options.description: Add a subject line above the letter saying Forms to complete. Helps readers who scan, but the hard opening sentence is still there underneath.

questions.question: A note field in the Tamil interface is limited to 20 characters, but Tamil script packs meaning into far fewer characters and uses few or no spaces, so a full name needs far more characters than the limit allows. What should be done?

options.label: Raise the limit per script
options.description: Use a higher character limit when the text is written in a script that packs meaning into fewer characters. Correct for all readers, but the rule has to be maintained per language.

options.label: Count visible letters not codes
options.description: Count the letters a reader sees rather than the internal code units, so the same name uses the same number of spaces in every language. Fair, but it still does not raise the limit.

options.label: Remove the limit
options.description: Remove the limit entirely for all scripts. Nobody is blocked, but the database column has a maximum and very long text must be truncated or stored elsewhere.

options.label: Keep the limit at 20
options.description: Keep the 20 character limit because the printed form also has a small box. Consistent with print, but a Tamil reader cannot complete the form at all.

questions.question: A service page promises: Your request will be resolved in 48 hours without exception. The team averages four days and has no way to meet the promise at peak times. What should the page say instead?

options.label: Give an honest typical time
options.description: We aim to reply within 5 working days. At busy times it can take longer. Nobody is misled, but some readers will be disappointed and may need a reason to stay.

options.label: Keep the promise
options.description: Keep 48 hours without exception because the service wants to look fast. No edit, but the service will miss its own published promise and trust falls when it does.

options.label: Make it vague
options.description: Say we will reply as soon as possible. Sounds safe, but it removes any time a reader can plan around, which was the point of the sentence.

options.label: Give two time bands
options.description: Say most requests are done in 2 days and complex ones can take 10 working days. More accurate still, but it asks the reader to judge which case they are in.

questions.question: A contacts list sorts Korean names alphabetically by the Roman letters, so Min appears under M and Han under H, while Korean readers expect the family name first, for example 한국어 이러. What should the sort use?

options.label: Sort in the reader's language
options.description: Sort in Korean script using Korean order, with the family name first, and offer a Roman sort as a second option. Correct and familiar, but it needs a sorted index per language.

options.label: Keep the Roman sort
options.description: Keep sorting by Roman letters for every language. One simple index, but Korean readers cannot find a name they know the way they expect.

options.label: Group by family name
options.description: Keep the Roman sort but display names family name first, for example Han Min. Readers recognise the shape, but the sort order is still wrong.

options.label: Offer no sort at all
options.description: Show the list in the order people were added. Nothing to maintain, but a long list becomes impossible to search by eye.

questions.question: A housing page says: Income received in the form of a non cash benefit is disregarded where it does not exceed 5 per cent of the applicable sum. What is the plain replacement?

options.label: Give a worked example
options.description: If your other income is 300 pounds a month, up to 15 pounds of it does not count towards your limit. Concrete and easy to test against, but it needs a new example for every limit in the rules.

options.label: Short sentence and number
options.description: We ignore up to 5 per cent of your other income. Shorter, but the words applicable sum and non cash benefit are gone, so the rule is harder to apply to an unusual case.

options.label: Keep the original sentence
options.description: Keep the original wording because it matches the legislation exactly. Safe for a legal challenge, but readers are asked to parse a sentence with three abstract nouns.

options.label: Send it to an adviser
options.description: Remove the rule from the page and say to ask an adviser. Simple page, but it removes information that many readers want to check themselves.
