questions.question: An emergency message shows the date 14/03/2026 and the interface language is Greek, where dates are written day first. A reader reads it as 3 March 2026. The interface language is Greek, Γεωργία, where dates are written day first. What should the change be?

options.label: Use a long date
options.description: Write 14 March 2026, or the Greek long form, instead of digits. No ambiguity for any reader, but it takes more space than three groups of numbers.

options.label: Use the month name
options.description: Write 14 Mar 2026 with a month name. Short and unambiguous, but three letter month names differ between languages and must be translated.

options.label: Label each part
options.description: Keep the numbers and put day, month and year under them. Keeps the space saving, but readers still have to work out which is which on a hurried message.

options.label: Keep the numbers only
options.description: Keep 14/03/2026 and rely on the language setting. Compact for an emergency banner, but the exact misreading it causes is the one that puts a person in the wrong place at the wrong time.

questions.question: A childcare page says: Eligibility is determined by reference to the statutory guidance, taking into account the circumstances of each individual application, and is subject to periodic review. What is the plain replacement?

options.label: One plain summary sentence
options.description: Each application is decided on its own facts, and the rules are checked from time to time. Says the essence in one line, but it no longer points to the statutory guidance that staff rely on.

options.label: Points, then the summary
options.description: List the three things that are checked, then add the summary sentence at the end. Most useful to a reader, but the order changes what staff think the page says.

options.label: Keep it, add a link
options.description: Keep the paragraph and link to the guidance. Reference is preserved, but the reader still has to decode the sentence to reach the link.

options.label: Remove the paragraph
options.description: Delete the paragraph and let the checklist speak for itself. Cleanest page, but it removes the statement that decisions are made case by case, which some readers rely on.

revision.feedback: Keep a plain summary first and move the statutory reference to the end so the reader meets the meaning before the citation.

questions.question: A Hindi warning line, खिातरमक जागुचानु, wraps in the middle of a word, splitting a single word across two lines and leaving a mark on the second line. What is the correct fix?

options.label: Never break inside a word
options.description: Set the rule that a line break may not fall inside a word for that script. Correct and general, but it can leave ragged right edges and taller paragraphs.

options.label: Add breaks by hand
options.description: Add line breaks by hand where they are needed. No rule change, but every new translation has to be checked again by hand.

questions.question: A recipe page shows 3/4 cup, roughly 180 ml, and a screen reader reads it as three forward slash four, which some readers take as three divided by four. What is the best fix?

options.label: Write three quarters
options.description: Write 3 quarters in words in the spoken version while keeping 3/4 on screen. Everyone understands it, but the spoken text and the visible text differ slightly.

options.label: Add a spoken name
options.description: Give the number a spoken name such as three quarters cup. The visible text stays as typed, and it has to be added to every fraction on the site by hand.

options.label: Rewrite in metric and words
options.description: Rewrite the recipe in metric measures and in words, for example about 180 ml. Fewer fractions overall, but it changes a familiar American recipe and needs care.

options.label: Keep the fraction
options.description: Keep 3/4 and add a note that fractions are written with a slash. No change to the recipe, but the note is one more thing to read before cooking.

options.label: Put the word first
options.description: Write about three quarters of a cup, putting the words before the numbers. Clear when read aloud, but the recipe no longer matches the printed book of recipes.

questions.question: A complaints page opens with a 190 word paragraph explaining the internal review process, and the contact details are in a table at the bottom. Readers report not reaching the contact details. What should be done?

options.label: Move contact details up
options.description: Put the phone number and the opening hours at the top, then the review process below. One move, and it is the change most likely to get a call made.

options.label: Cut the review paragraph
options.description: Cut the 190 word paragraph to two sentences about what happens after a complaint. Shorter page, but the detail about timescales is lost unless it is kept elsewhere.

options.label: Steps plus a contact link
options.description: Turn the review process into four numbered steps and keep a contact link at the top. Structured and clear, but it still does not tell a reader how long the whole thing takes.

options.label: Keep the page
options.description: Keep the page exactly as it is because the process description is legally required wording. No edit, but the same readers keep missing the contact details.

questions.question: An alcohol policy page uses 🍺 to mean the legal drinking age and 👵 to mean older residents. Readers report that the glass and the older person emoji are confusing and dated. What should replace them?

options.label: Use words, not pictures
options.description: Write the age and the age group in words, for example 18 or over and residents over 65. Unambiguous and timeless, but the page loses its informal visual style.

options.label: Use neutral icons
options.description: Use a neutral drink icon and a neutral age icon with the number beside them. Keeps a visual cue, but the numbers still have to be written out.

options.label: Keep the emoji
options.description: Keep the two emoji because readers already recognise them from other pages. No edit, but the reported confusion stays and the style ages with the interface.

options.label: Caption every picture
options.description: Keep the emoji and add a spoken name to each one. Helps screen reader users only, and the confusion for sighted readers is not addressed.

questions.question: A form ends with: By submitting this form you confirm that the information provided is accurate and complete to the best of your knowledge and belief. What is the plain replacement?

questions.question: A pull quote wraps a sentence in straight double quotes, and that sentence contains an apostrophe in a name, so the two marks look the same on screen and the sentence is hard to read. What is the correct fix?

options.label: Use nested curly quotes
options.description: Use a curly opening and closing quote around the sentence and a different mark inside for the apostrophe. Standard practice, but it needs care on every language version.

options.label: Reword to avoid inner mark
options.description: Reword the sentence so there is no apostrophe inside the quotation. Simple and it looks right everywhere, but the sentence may lose a natural turn of phrase.

options.label: Use a real quote block
options.description: Set the sentence as a block quote with no quotation marks at all. Cleaner on screen, but a screen reader user loses the signal that these are someone else's words.

options.label: Keep the straight marks
options.description: Keep the straight marks as they are. No change, but the pull quote looks like a line of code rather than a quotation.

options.label: Use single outer quotes
options.description: Wrap the sentence in single curly quotes and keep the apostrophe inside as written. A common typographic solution, but the outer mark is less distinct on a dim screen.

options.label: Drop the quote on mobile
options.description: Show the quote as plain indented text on small screens and keep the marks on larger ones. Cleaner on a phone, but the two versions are no longer the same sentence.

questions.question: A serious safety notice about a gas leak opens with three smiling faces 😀😁😃 above the text. Readers say the notice looks unserious and one person turned the page early. What should the change be?

options.label: Remove them
options.description: Take the three faces out of the notice and let the warning stand on its own words. Appropriate tone for an emergency, but it removes the only visual cue that the page is about something urgent.

options.label: Use a warning symbol
options.description: Replace the faces with a plain warning symbol and the word Warning in large text. Signals urgency without cheerfulness, but the symbol still has to be described for a screen reader.

options.label: Keep the faces
options.description: Keep the faces because the tone is meant to be friendly and reassuring. No edit, but the reported reaction stands and the notice is about a hazard, not a greeting.

options.label: Use one neutral face
options.description: Use one neutral face, such as 😐, to keep a human tone. A compromise on tone, but it still distracts from the words at the moment the reader most needs them.

options.label: Use a top warning banner
options.description: Put the warning in a full width banner at the very top of the page with a symbol and the word Warning. Impossible to miss, but it pushes the page content down on a small screen.

options.description: Provides strong isolation but raises cost and migration complexity at scale.

options.label: Route by tenant region
